rv.q: In any good enough production, “Our Town” is titanic: beyond time and brutal.
By the end, Our Town has revealed itself to be a devastating, frighteningly profound meditation on moments that are at once insignificant and infinitely full.
Life is fragile and fleeting, and love is all that matters.
Echoes of those parts in Parsons’s excellent performance stir up a host of greater resonances.
Here, Leon does beautiful and evocative work updating the everyday Americans “Our Town” appears to reflect. But even widening the definition of ordinary suggests there is such a thing.
Jim Parsons brings a gentle, contemplative presence to the Stage Manager role, while Katie Holmes delivers a touching performance as Mrs. Webb in this affecting revival.
Mr. Leon’s “Our Town” is polished and marked by moments of humor and melancholy, but they do not cohere into a powerfully affecting production.
Director Kenny Leon's conceptually laudable but scrambled production of the revered theatrical staple 'Our Town' finds its divine core, but lacks connection.
Parsons is excellent but otherwise the forced re-interpretations of character, time, place and beliefs often fall short.
It’s not painful, but it’s far from revelatory.
So, why, if it is Our town, is director Kenny Leon’s staging of “Our Town” among the most uninvolving and anemic I have ever seen?
This feels a lot more like our town than Our Town ever has.

Grounded by Jim Parsons’ no-nonsense, emotionally charged performance as the Stage Manager and a multicultural cast split racially right down the middle, this is an Our Town perfectly suited for our times.
At Kenny Leon’s very welcome Our Town, patrons are guaranteed to appreciate Thornton Wilder’s genius every, every minute.
He seems to share an existential grief with Parson’s Stage Manager, and the production strikes a similarly melancholy tone.
Ultimately, Wilder’s words remain the magic; the progression from a day to a wedding to a funeral a guaranteed gut punch.

Unfortunately, a lack of chemistry between the two other main characters, young lovers George Gibbs (Ephraim Sykes) and Emily Webb (Zoey Deutch), keeps the production from achieving a certain pathos overall.
Mr. Leon’s aim, clearly, is to also make us wish for a better world, and as it’s relayed here, that goal doesn’t seem at all incongruous with Wilder’s vision.

If ”Our Town” at the Barrymore is not a production for the ages, it’s as good an introduction to the play as any for somebody who has never seen it – and surely there are such people, even in America.
There are so many townsfolk to look at and so many ideas to linger over here, but the ultimate irony of this production is that it feels rushed.
A bigger one lies in Kenny Leon's decision to bring in a contemporary perspective that is in conflict with the underlying "truth" of the place and time in which Our Town takes place.
No offense to Mr. Albee, but “Our Town,” has always struck me as alternately boring, banal and, at the end, admittedly rather moving.
In making the play more of a sprint, meanings and nuance—and just the time you need to spend with characters for them to imprint themselves—have been lost.
An extreme condescension, however, enters into the picture with several of the female actors’ performances thanks to the costumes, by Dede Ayite, which are dreadful.
Kenny Leon's Broadway revival…can't quite make up its mind about several key matters.
But when you walk out of a revival thinking how thrilling the play was the last time you saw it—well that’s a problem, isn’t it?
Wilder’s brilliant playwriting shines through, reaffirming my widely held conviction that this is America’s greatest play.
This Broadway revival will be remembered long after it closes and ensures that “Our Town” is positively everyone’s town.
And this is a thoughtful, well-crafted production that captures that spirit, and nudges it forward a bit for an American public that Thornton Wilder could never have envisioned.
For his part, Parsons disappointed in that he was too similar to other characters he’s played.

cn.t: Critics find Kenny Leon's revival of Wilder's classic emotionally stirring but uneven, with Jim Parsons' Stage Manager and the diverse casting praised, though some feel it lacks the cohesion to fully honor the timeless material.

vr.q: I found this production to be much like the town it's about: simple, wholesome, but not remarkably memorable except for maybe one sensory surprise toward the end.
